plan.contextChunk: This figure is a plain black-and-white line drawing of a trough in oblique three-dimensional view, with no shading or color. The body is a long open channel whose cross section is a parabola: the near end at the left is drawn as a U-shaped curve narrowing to a rounded point at the bottom, the same curve repeats at the far end on the right, and straight lines join the two rims along the length so the opening runs uniformly from end to end. Three measurements are marked. A double-headed vertical arrow inside the near end spans from the top rim down to the lowest point of the curve, labeled 18 in. A label along the upper front edge reads 3 ft for the length. A short segment across the far end of the top rim reads 12 in for the width across the opening. The flat rectangle formed by the rims and connecting lines represents the open water surface. Giving depth, length, and top width against a visible parabolic profile supplies just the quantities needed to fit an equation to the cross section and then write the water's surface area as a function of its depth.

elements: near-end (left) parabolic cross-section curve, U-shaped with vertex at the bottom and rim points at top, drawn true in the screen plane
far-end (right) identical parabolic cross-section curve, offset up-right along the receding length
front-top rim line joining the near and far left rim points along the length
back-top rim line joining the near and far right rim points along the length
bottom generator line joining the near and far parabola vertices along the length
open top rectangle bounded by the two rim lines and the two top chords (the empty water-surface plane)
water volume fill: parabolic-segment area at the near end plus an extruded semi-transparent body up to the water depth
water surface rectangle (horizontal plane) at the current depth, outlined and lightly filled blue
water cross-section line (horizontal chord) across the near-end parabola at the current depth
vertical double-headed arrow inside the near end spanning rim to vertex, labeled 18 in
length label 3 ft placed along the front-top rim line
width label 12 in placed across the far-end top rim
cross-section view: x-axis (width, in) and y-axis (depth, in) with tick marks
cross-section view: fitted parabola curve through (0,0), (-6,18), (6,18)
cross-section view: horizontal water line at the slider depth with its width bracket
cross-section view: shaded parabolic water segment below the water line

interactions.label: Water depth (in)
interactions.teaches: Raising the fill line widens the water surface chord inside the parabola, showing the surface width is a function of depth (width = 2*sqrt(2*depth) for the default profile), not a fixed 12 in

interactions.label: Trough length (ft)
interactions.teaches: Stretching the channel lengthens the water-surface rectangle while the cross-section stays fixed, showing surface area = (cross-section width at that depth) times length

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching to the cross-section graph reveals the fitted parabola y = 0.5*x^2 determined by the 18 in depth and 12 in top width, connecting the physical channel to its equation

interactions.label: Cross-section profile
interactions.teaches: Editing the profile curve (or imagining new depth/width constraints) redraws the end parabola and the 3D fill, so the water width at any depth is derived from the entered curve rather than assumed

demo_steps.title: Default trough
demo_steps.narration: The empty parabolic channel shows its three given measures: 18 in deep, 12 in across the top, 3 ft long. The open top rectangle is the would-be water surface.

demo_steps.title: Raise the water
demo_steps.narration: Drag depth to 18 in: the surface chord grows to the full 12 in. At 9 in the chord is only about 8.5 in wide, proving width depends on depth.

demo_steps.title: Lengthen the channel
demo_steps.narration: Increase length to 6 ft. The cross-section is unchanged but the blue water-surface rectangle doubles in area, isolating length as the second factor in surface area.

demo_steps.title: Read the equation
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to Cross-section: the same 18 in by 12 in end becomes the parabola y = 0.5*x^2 with the water line drawn at the chosen depth, ready to write surface area as a function of depth.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: 1 in = 0.1 world unit. Near-end parabola lies in the screen XY plane at z=0 with vertex at origin (0,0,0), rim points at (-0.6, 1.8, 0) and (0.6, 1.8, 0); default profile y = 0.5*x^2 in inches (so at y=18, x=±6). Far end is the same curve translated to z = length (3 ft = 36 in = 3.6 units by default). +X = screen-right (width), +Y = screen-up (depth), +Z = receding diagonal up-right (length). Water fill: horizontal plane at y = depth*0.1, clipped to the parabola, extruded along z; surface rectangle width = 2*sqrt(2*depth)*0.1 by length. Labels in dark grey #333333; line work near-black #1a1a1a; water #2a7fd4 at ~0.25 opacity with a stronger #1a66cc surface outline. In Cross-section view use a flat front-on plot: x-axis -7..7 in, y-axis 0..20 in, parabola sampled over x in [-6,6].
interactionPlan.notes: Oblique renderer uses a fixed standard pose; do not add orbit. Recompute the water chord width numerically at runtime by scanning the entered f(x) over its domain for the x where f(x)=depth (bisection/linear scan), so an edited equation correctly drives both the 2D curve and the 3D fill width. Keep both the 3D trough group and the 2D cross-section group in the scene and show/hide on the toggle rather than rebuilding. Clip the parabola and water body to y <= 18 in (1.8 units) so an edited curve that exceeds the rim does not overflow the channel. Surface area readout = width_at_depth(in) * length(in).

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for water depth: the learner raises and lowers a horizontal fill line inside the parabolic cross section and the water surface width changes, making clear that width is a function of depth rather than a constant.
- Toggle between 3D trough and cross-section graph: the learner switches from the channel view to the fitted parabola using 18 in depth and 12 in top width, making clear how the physical dimensions determine the equation for the end profile.
- Slider for trough length: the learner adjusts the 3 ft length and the water surface rectangle extends while the cross-section stays fixed, making clear how cross-sectional width and length combine to determine surface area.
- Equation input for the trough cross-section: learner edits a parabolic profile or the 18 in depth and 12 in width constraints; the cross-section and 3D trough fill redraw so width is derived from the entered curve.

authoredContext:
For example, suppose the Sustainability Club builds a water runoff collector in the shape of a parabolic trough as shown in the figure. We can use the information in the figure to find the surface area of the water in the trough as a function of the depth of the water.

Diagram of a parabolic trough that is 18” in height, 3’ in length, and 12” in width.

Because it will be helpful to have an equation for the parabolic cross-sectional shape, we will impose a coordinate system at the cross section, with x measured horizontally and y measured vertically, with the origin at the vertex of the parabola. See the figure.

Place the 18 in depth double-arrow on the near parabolic face and render '12 in' as a width dimension across the top opening to match the source annotation style

interactions.label: Trough length (ft)

interactions.label: View

demo_steps.title: Default trough
demo_steps.narration: The empty parabolic channel shows its three given measures: 18 in deep, 12 in across the top, 3 ft long. The open top rectangle is the would-be water surface.

demo_steps.title: Raise the water
demo_steps.narration: Drag depth to 18 in: the surface chord grows to the full 12 in. At 9 in the chord is only about 8.5 in wide, proving width depends on depth.

demo_steps.title: Lengthen the channel
demo_steps.narration: Increase length to 6 ft. The cross-section is unchanged but the blue water-surface rectangle doubles in area, isolating length as the second factor in surface area.

demo_steps.title: Read the equation
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to Cross-section: the same 18 in by 12 in end becomes the parabola y = 0.5*x^2 with the water line drawn at the chosen depth, ready to write surface area as a function of depth.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: 1 in = 0.1 world unit. Near-end parabola lies in the screen XY plane at z=0 with vertex at origin (0,0,0), rim points at (-0.6, 1.8, 0) and (0.6, 1.8, 0); default profile y = 0.5*x^2 in inches (so at y=18, x=±6). Far end is the same curve translated to z = length (3 ft = 36 in = 3.6 units by default). +X = screen-right (width), +Y = screen-up (depth), +Z = receding diagonal up-right (length). Water fill: horizontal plane at y = depth*0.1, clipped to the parabola, extruded along z; surface rectangle width = 2*sqrt(2*depth)*0.1 by length. Labels in dark grey #333333; line work near-black #1a1a1a; water #2a7fd4 at ~0.25 opacity with a stronger #1a66cc surface outline. In Cross-section view use a flat front-on plot: x-axis -7..7 in, y-axis 0..20 in, parabola sampled over x in [-6,6].
interactionPlan.notes: Oblique renderer uses a fixed standard pose; do not add orbit. Recompute the water chord width numerically at runtime by scanning the entered f(x) over its domain for the x where f(x)=depth (bisection/linear scan), so an edited equation correctly drives both the 2D curve and the 3D fill width. Keep both the 3D trough group and the 2D cross-section group in the scene and show/hide on the toggle rather than rebuilding. Clip the parabola and water body to y <= 18 in (1.8 units) so an edited curve that exceeds the rim does not overflow the channel. Surface area readout = width_at_depth(in) * length(in).

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure is a plain black-and-white line drawing of a trough in oblique three-dimensional view, with no shading or color. The body is a long open channel whose cross section is a parabola: the near end at the left is drawn as a U-shaped curve narrowing to a rounded point at the bottom, the same curve repeats at the far end on the right, and straight lines join the two rims along the length so the opening runs uniformly from end to end. Three measurements are marked. A double-headed vertical arrow inside the near end spans from the top rim down to the lowest point of the curve, labeled 18 in. A label along the upper front edge reads 3 ft for the length. A short segment across the far end of the top rim reads 12 in for the width across the opening. The flat rectangle formed by the rims and connecting lines represents the open water surface. Giving depth, length, and top width against a visible parabolic profile supplies just the quantities needed to fit an equation to the cross section and then write the water's surface area as a function of its depth.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for water depth: the learner raises and lowers a horizontal fill line inside the parabolic cross section and the water surface width changes, making clear that width is a function of depth rather than a constant.
- Toggle between 3D trough and cross-section graph: the learner switches from the channel view to the fitted parabola using 18 in depth and 12 in top width, making clear how the physical dimensions determine the equation for the end profile.
- Slider for trough length: the learner adjusts the 3 ft length and the water surface rectangle extends while the cross-section stays fixed, making clear how cross-sectional width and length combine to determine surface area.
- Equation input for the trough cross-section: learner edits a parabolic profile or the 18 in depth and 12 in width constraints; the cross-section and 3D trough fill redraw so width is derived from the entered curve.
